interfaces: ControlledMergeResult { taskId, lifecycleState: 'DONE', pullRequestNumber, sourceRevision, mergeCommitSha, evidenceLineageId, evidenceSequence }

ControlledMergeErrorCode = INVALID_REQUEST | TASK_NOT_FOUND | TASK_STATE_NOT_MERGEABLE | BRANCH_REJECTED | NOT_MERGE_READY | HEAD_CHANGED | MERGE_PROVIDER_FAILED | MERGE_NOT_CONFIRMED | EVIDENCE_REJECTED | LIFECYCLE_REJECTED | LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED | STATE_CONFLICT | STATE_IO_FAILED

LockIdentity { lockId, ownerId, runId, canonicalBranch }, the full assignment identity captured at merge() entry and compared in full before release
ControlledMergePullRequestPort.findPullRequestsByHead(head): Promise<readonly ControlledMergePullRequestRecord[]>, every matching PR for the branch, any state, not only the most recent

ControlledMergeTaskLock.withLock<T>(taskId, fn: (assertHeld: () => void) => Promise<T>): Promise<T>, an async-critical-section variant of BOOT-018's/BOOT-019's/BOOT-020's/BOOT-021's own synchronous task-lock port; assertHeld is a fencing check fn calls before every side-effecting operation

FileControlledMergeTaskLock(root, options?: { staleLockMs?, heartbeatIntervalMs? }) concrete ControlledMergeTaskLock over .agent/state/lifecycle/<taskId>.lifecycle.lock, sharing the lifecycle root FileControlledMergeStateStore uses, with a periodic heartbeat refreshing the held lock file so a long-running critical section is never mistaken for an abandoned one
GitHubControlledMergePullRequestOperations(options) concrete ControlledMergePullRequestPort adapter over the GitHub REST pulls/merge endpoints

behavioralConstraints: merge() checks whether the task is already DONE (a pure, side-effect-free read of the persisted lifecycle record) before ever acquiring the task lock, so the idempotent DONE path can never be blocked by lock contention — a concurrent in-progress attempt, or an abandoned-but-not-yet-stale lock file — from returning already-persisted evidence; every other entry state re-checks DONE once more immediately after acquiring the lock (covering a concurrent caller reaching DONE in the gap between the unlocked pre-check and lock acquisition), then proceeds with the lock held

for any non-DONE entry state, merge() acquires an exclusive per-task lock (ControlledMergeTaskLock.withLock) around its entire read-decide-write critical section — including every awaited branch/readiness/provider call — before doing anything else, so two concurrent merge() calls for the same task never interleave; a concurrent call finds the lock held and is rejected as STATE_CONFLICT. While held, the lock file's mtime is periodically refreshed (a heartbeat, well inside the stale-reclaim threshold, via a metadata-only touch that never removes the lock file) so a critical section whose readiness/provider calls legitimately run long is never mistaken for an abandoned holder and reclaimed by a concurrent caller out from under it. withLock also hands fn an assertHeld fencing callback; merge()/finalize()/resumeBookkeeping()/completeFromMerged() call it immediately before each individual side-effecting operation in turn — the mergePullRequest call, again immediately after that call returns, again at finalize()'s own entry, again immediately before the evidence write itself (record()), again immediately before the MERGE_READY -> MERGED save, again before releaseLockIfPresent, and again before the MERGED -> DONE save — rather than only once at the top of the whole chain: none of these steps contains its own await, but each is still a real filesystem operation taking non-zero wall-clock time during which a concurrent process's own reclaim can complete regardless of this process's own JS scheduling, so a single check at the top would not bound the risk to any one operation. Each assertHeld call throws STATE_CONFLICT if this holder's token no longer matches the lock file's content, aborting before that specific side effect rather than completing it alongside a second, legitimate holder

merge() only ever acts on a task whose persisted lifecycle currentState is MERGE_READY, MERGED, or DONE; any other state is rejected as TASK_STATE_NOT_MERGEABLE before any branch, readiness, or provider call

a task already DONE returns its persisted ipt.merge-evidence record (read through control-plane.evidence-store's mergeEvidenceLineageId(taskId)) unchanged, with no branch, readiness, provider, lock, or lifecycle-state write of any kind

for a task in MERGE_READY only, immediately after confirming that state, the assignment lock's full identity (lockId, ownerId, runId, canonicalBranch — not lockId alone, since the assignment-lock contract does not guarantee a lockId is never reused by a later acquisition) is captured once via ControlledMergeLockStore.get(); a read failure here is normalized to a recoverable LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED rather than propagating raw. This captured identity, never a freshly re-read lock, is what completion later attempts to release for this fresh attempt

a task already MERGED (a prior call wrote merge evidence and the MERGED lifecycle transition but was interrupted before lock release/DONE) resumes purely from its persisted merge evidence: no branch check, no merge-readiness evaluation, no pull-request provider call, and — unlike the MERGE_READY path — no fresh assignment-lock snapshot of any kind runs on this path; the lock identity to release is instead read from that same evidence record's own assignmentLockAtMerge field (see below), since whatever lock happens to be active right now may belong to a completely different, later assignment of the same task

for a task in MERGE_READY, the canonical branch and exact current revision are resolved strictly through the unmodified control-plane.git-branch-lifecycle adapter; a Git branch mismatch or Git failure (including a failure resolving the revision itself) is normalized to BRANCH_REJECTED before any other check

before evaluating merge readiness, every pull request for the canonical branch (any state, not only open, not only the most recent, and not only the first page of results) is looked up once via findPullRequestsByHead, and the highest-numbered candidate — if any — reporting merged=true with headSha equal to the revision the task's own MERGE_READY lifecycle-history event actually approved (never the branch's live current head) AND baseRef equal to the configured integrationTarget (default 'main') is selected — the highest-numbered such match, not merely the first one encountered in whatever order the provider port returns candidates, since ControlledMergePullRequestPort makes no ordering promise and, when both a historical reverted PR and the task's actual newer approval happen to both report merged=true for the same revision/base (the ordinary case this shortcut exists for, not only the adversarial reused-SHA scenario below), an adapter that simply returns the older one first must not cause it to be selected over the genuinely current match; searching by the approved revision rather than the live head matters because a confirmed merge can be followed by an unrelated push before evidence is recorded, in which case the live head no longer matches the merged PR at all and the merged/closed PR is equally invisible to the normal readiness path below, permanently stranding an already-successful merge otherwise. The base check is part of this same selection predicate, not a filter applied only after find() has already committed to the first head-matching candidate, since a more-recently-created merged PR against an unrelated base could otherwise be selected first and hide the actual integration-target merge behind it. Scanning every candidate across every page (rather than only the single most-recently-created one, or only the first 100 results) matters for crash recovery specifically: a stray, unrelated PR created after the genuinely approved one, or the genuine merge sitting beyond a long-lived branch's first 100 historical PRs, must never hide the actual merged PR a prior, interrupted attempt already produced. A selected candidate is additionally distrusted — the shortcut is not taken, even though the candidate itself satisfies every field of the selection predicate — when any other, not-merged candidate for the branch targets the same integrationTarget base and carries a strictly higher PR number, whether that other candidate is still open or has since been closed without merging (rejected, superseded, abandoned): a canonical branch belongs to one task's approval at a time, so a higher-numbered, same-base, not-merged PR is necessarily a newer pull request than the matched one, meaning the matched candidate can only be a historical PR (for example one that was squash-merged and later reverted on the integration target) whose merged=true/headSha/baseRef fields still, correctly, describe that past event even though it does not represent this attempt's approval; trusting it regardless would record a stale merge commit and complete the task while the real approval never lands (or, if that real approval has itself become unmergeable, incorrectly complete the task at all). This distrust check cannot currently catch a narrower case — the actual approved PR retargeted away from integrationTarget after readiness last evaluated it — since a PR's current baseRef alone cannot distinguish retargeted-away-from-main from always-targeted-a-different-base-and-genuinely-unrelated-to-this-approval (the latter must never count as superseding); closing that narrower gap would require persisting the approved PR's own identity at MERGE_READY time, which is out of scope for this controller alone since three separate, already-shipped review modules (not this one) write that transition. That selected candidate is otherwise trusted as a confirmed prior result — skipping merge-readiness evaluation and the mergePullRequest call entirely; when no such candidate exists (including when the task has no MERGE_READY history event to search by at all), the shortcut is not taken and control falls through to the normal readiness-evaluate path, which safely rejects (the merged/closed PR is invisible to findOpenPullRequests, so evaluate() reports PULL_REQUEST_NOT_FOUND) rather than trusting a claim it cannot verify

when the pull request is not already merged (or the already-merged shortcut's gating fails), control-plane.merge-readiness's evaluate() is invoked for the exact task; its own resolved revision is compared against the revision this controller already resolved, and any mismatch is rejected as HEAD_CHANGED before ready is even inspected
a ready=false merge-readiness result is rejected as NOT_MERGE_READY, carrying every reason's message; mergePullRequest is never called in this case

a ready=true merge-readiness result's pullRequestNumber is rejected as NOT_MERGE_READY unless it is a positive integer (not merely non-null): ControlledMergeReadinessPort is a public port any caller may satisfy with a different implementation, and a non-positive or fractional value would otherwise still be fetched (getPullRequest) and merged through the provider, only being caught afterward when the merge-evidence schema rejects it as not a well-formed integer >= 1 — stranding an already-irreversible provider merge in MERGE_READY; this boundary check runs before the pre-merge recheck or mergePullRequest call, the same provider-neutral independence already applied to an empty merge-commit SHA

immediately before calling mergePullRequest, the exact pull request readiness selected is re-fetched by number (getPullRequest), never by the any-state/most-recent-by-head lookup findPullRequestsByHead uses — a branch can legitimately carry more than one pull request across its history (for example a stray closed PR against a different base created more recently than the genuinely open, approved one), and a most-recent-by-head lookup could return that unrelated PR instead of the one readiness actually evaluated; any change in the fetched PR's merged status, open/closed state, head SHA, or base (relative to the merge-readiness result already evaluated and the configured integrationTarget) is rejected as HEAD_CHANGED without calling the merge provider — the base check specifically catches a PR retargeted away from integrationTarget after readiness evaluated it, since GitHub's merge sha parameter protects only the head revision, never the base, and the state check specifically catches a PR closed without merging in that same gap, since its merged flag, head, and base can all remain unchanged even though it is no longer mergeable

mergePullRequest is called with the exact expected head SHA; a real GitHub adapter passes it as the merge endpoint's own sha parameter, so a head that moved between this controller's last local check and GitHub's own processing of the request is rejected server-side (HTTP 409) and mapped to HEAD_CHANGED here, never silently merging a different commit

a mergePullRequest response reporting merged=false, or reporting merged=true with an empty sha, is rejected as MERGE_NOT_CONFIRMED; the empty-sha check runs at the controller's own provider-neutral boundary immediately after mergePullRequest returns, independent of whatever check (if any) the concrete port adapter behind it performs, since ControlledMergePullRequestPort is a public port any caller may satisfy with a different implementation; no evidence is recorded and no lifecycle transition occurs, leaving the task MERGE_READY and safe to retry

a provider failure (network, HTTP, or malformed response) while finding, fetching, or merging a pull request is normalized to MERGE_PROVIDER_FAILED (or, for GitHub's own 409 head-mismatch response, to HEAD_CHANGED) and leaves the task's persisted lifecycle state and evidence completely unchanged

only once a merge is confirmed (either freshly, or already-merged and read back) is merge evidence finalized: if a current ipt.merge-evidence record already exists for this task, is a fully well-formed ipt.merge-evidence payload for this exact task and revision (the same structural check resolvePinnedEvidence already requires of a resumed record — routed through evidenceStore.validate(), the evidence store's own full schema-document validation boundary, not a hand-maintained partial field list, so a wrong schemaVersion, a fractional pullRequestNumber, a missing evidenceId/policyDecisionReference/recordedAt, or any other schema violation is caught the same way record() itself would catch it, in addition to schemaId/taskId and a well-formed pullRequestNumber/mergeCommitSha — not only a bare comparison of three field values, which a null or otherwise malformed stored payload could previously fail non-obviously, including throwing a raw TypeError on a null payload rather than ever reaching a typed error), the stored record's own wrapper lineageId exactly equals the lineage this call itself derived and its wrapper sequence is a well-formed integer >= 1 (evidenceStore.getHistory reads these two fields directly off the stored file's own JSON content with no cross-check against the directory it was actually found in, and a reused record's evidenceRef is built directly from them — a corrupted wrapper would otherwise still be reused to persist a MERGED/DONE evidenceRef a later idempotent read can never resolve back, even with a perfectly valid payload), and whose revisionIdentity, pullRequestNumber, and mergeCommitSha all match exactly (a prior attempt recorded it and then crashed before the MERGE_READY -> MERGED transition persisted), that exact record is reused rather than appending a duplicate; a current record that fails this check is never reused regardless of how it became malformed, and finalize() instead falls through to writing a fresh, valid record, self-healing past the corruption rather than trusting it or hard-failing on it, and the lock identity carried forward to completion is that reused record's own assignmentLockAtMerge — never this retry's freshly captured live snapshot, since the retry's own snapshot could reflect a completely different, later-reassigned actor; otherwise exactly one new record is written, naming the task, the merged source revision, the pull-request number, the merge commit SHA, a policyDecisionReference string, and the assignment-lock identity (lockId, ownerId, runId, canonicalBranch, or null) active at this exact moment as assignmentLockAtMerge, and that live-captured identity is what completion uses. A filesystem/I/O failure from the evidence store's own record() or getCurrent() call at this point (a full disk, an unwritable evidence directory) is caught and normalized to a recoverable EVIDENCE_REJECTED, never left to propagate as a raw, uncaught exception — the confirmed merge remains safely resumable once the underlying I/O problem clears. Either way this record is written (or confirmed to already exist) before the MERGE_READY -> MERGED lifecycle transition, so that transition's own evidenceRef always names an already-persisted record, and at most one current merge-evidence record ever exists per confirmed merge

resuming a MERGED task, and answering an already-DONE task's idempotent read, both resolve evidence by parsing the exact `${lineageId}@${sequence}` named by that task's own MERGED (respectively DONE) lifecycle-history event's evidenceRef, rejecting it as EVIDENCE_REJECTED unless the parsed lineageId is exactly this task's own mergeEvidenceLineageId(taskId), and reading that precise sequence back through getHistory() — never merely getCurrent()'s current record for the lineage — so a hypothetical later, unrelated write to the same lineage can never silently change what an already-persisted transition is understood to describe. The fetched record is further verified to actually be ipt.merge-evidence for this exact task and this exact event's revisionIdentity, with a usable pullRequestNumber and mergeCommitSha, before any of its fields are trusted; a syntactically well-formed evidenceRef that resolves to a record failing that check is rejected as EVIDENCE_REJECTED rather than cast and used. On the MERGED-resume path, the record's assignmentLockAtMerge field (parsed defensively — anything other than a well-formed { lockId, ownerId, runId, canonicalBranch } shape or a genuine null resolves to null, meaning nothing is released) supplies the lock identity for completion, never a fresh ControlledMergeLockStore.get() snapshot

the assignment lock is released only as a best-effort, idempotent step after the MERGED transition persists, and only ever targets the exact identity tied to the original merge attempt (lockId, ownerId, runId, canonicalBranch together) — captured live at entry for a fresh MERGE_READY attempt, read back from assignmentLockAtMerge for a MERGED resume, or (on finalize()'s reuse path) read from the reused evidence's own assignmentLockAtMerge: a read failure against the concrete lock store itself (an I/O error or malformed lock file) at the completion-time re-read, or a raw throw from release() itself, is caught and normalized to a recoverable LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED rather than propagating as a raw exception. If the currently active lock (re-read at release time) is missing, release() is never called; if that lock's four identity fields no longer match — because it was reassigned to a different actor's legitimate assignment (whether while the original call was still in flight, or at any point before a later resume ran), including a later assignment that happens to reuse the same lockId — release() is likewise never called, and no error is raised for either case. When the full identity still matches, release() is invoked regardless of that record's own reported status: a status already 'RELEASED' is not treated as proof the release already fully completed, since the concrete store's own release() writes that status, appends an audit event, and archives the record as three separate steps, and a failure between the first and the other two would otherwise leave that record permanently unarchived and abandoned. The release() call itself passes the captured ownerId/runId/canonicalBranch as expectedOwnerId/expectedRunId/expectedCanonicalBranch, an atomic compare-and-swap guard the concrete lock store checks against the exact same read it uses to decide whether to mutate anything — closing the gap between this controller's own separate, earlier full-identity check and the actual release call, during which a stale-recovery reusing this exact lockId for a different, legitimate owner (permitted by the assignment-lock contract) would otherwise still pass a lockId-only match inside release() itself. A rejection other than LOCK_NOT_FOUND/LOCK_ID_MISMATCH from this call surfaces as LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED, which blocks the MERGED -> DONE transition but leaves the already-persisted MERGED state and evidence fully resumable on a later call
the MERGED -> DONE transition is attempted only after lock release succeeds or is treated as already-handled; a rejected DONE transition is surfaced as LIFECYCLE_REJECTED

DONE is reachable through this module only by way of a confirmed merge result feeding a persisted merge-evidence record feeding the MERGE_READY -> MERGED -> DONE lifecycle transitions; there is no path that reaches DONE from any other evidence or from a caller-supplied override
invariants: this is the only module the bootstrap defines that transitions a task through MERGED or to DONE; no other module writes either state

merge() never calls the merge provider more than once for the same confirmed merge: a resume after any interruption point either finds the pull request already merged (via findPullRequestsByHead, scanning every candidate) or reads back already-persisted merge evidence, never re-invoking mergePullRequest
merge() never records merge evidence or writes a lifecycle transition for a merge that failed, was rejected, or was not confirmed by the provider

task-domain logic (ControlledMergeController) depends only on its typed dependency-port interfaces; it never inspects GitHub-specific response shapes or another module's internal storage layout directly

a branch, evidence, lifecycle, lock, or provider failure that occurs before a merge is confirmed always leaves the task's persisted lifecycle state exactly as it was found, so every such failure is safely retryable

completion never releases an assignment lock other than the exact full identity (lockId, ownerId, runId, canonicalBranch) tied to the original merge attempt itself; a lock reassigned to a different actor — even one that happens to reuse the same lockId — is never released by any call, whether that reassignment happened while the original call was still in flight or at any point before a later resume completed bookkeeping for it
at most one current ipt.merge-evidence record ever exists per task, even across a crash between recording it and persisting the MERGED transition
the DONE path never acquires ControlledMergeTaskLock; only MERGE_READY and MERGED entry states do

a MERGED or DONE task's resolved evidence always matches the exact sequence its own lifecycle-history event names and is always verified to be valid ipt.merge-evidence for that exact task and revision, never merely whatever the lineage's getCurrent() reports as current and never a syntactically valid but semantically unrelated record trusted on faith
the already-merged shortcut's candidate search always uses the revision the task's own MERGE_READY lifecycle-history event approved, never the branch's live current head

the task-lock heartbeat's refresh never removes, renames, or recreates the lock file — it only verifies ownership by content and then bumps the file's own filesystem mtime via a metadata-only touch — so the lock path remains continuously present, and continuously EEXIST to any concurrent tryCreate(), for the entire time a holder legitimately owns it. The assertHeld fencing check, called immediately before each individual side-effecting operation (never only once at the top of the chain that performs them), narrows the remaining residual risk further by aborting a holder that has nonetheless lost the lock, rather than eliminating that risk outright (no plain file lock without OS-level flock/fcntl or a lease service can)

a read failure against the concrete assignment-lock store, or a raw throw from release() itself, is always normalized to a typed ControlledMergeError (LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED), never left to propagate as a raw exception, whether it occurs at the entry-time lock snapshot, the completion-time release check, or the release call itself
finalize()'s evidence-reuse path always carries forward the reused record's own assignmentLockAtMerge as the identity to release, never this call's own freshly captured live snapshot

a currently active lock record whose identity still matches this call's own is always passed to release(), regardless of whether its reported status already reads RELEASED, so an interrupted prior release (status flipped but not yet archived/audited) is retried rather than assumed complete

FileControlledMergeTaskLock's own release() claims the lock path via an atomic rename before verifying its content is this holder's own token, mirroring reclaimIfStale's claim technique, rather than a plain read-then-unlink: a bare read-then-unlink cannot rule out a concurrent reclaimer replacing the lock file in between, which would otherwise delete that replacement's fresh lock rather than this (already-gone) holder's own, letting a third caller acquire the lock while the replacement's own callback is still active. That claiming rename still leaves the lock path briefly absent while release() decides what to do with what it captured, so release() additionally holds a reservation marker file at a fixed, well-known path (checked by tryCreate() both immediately before its own exclusive-create write and immediately after, rolling its own write back if the marker appeared in that narrow gap) for its entire duration: without it, a concurrent tryCreate() — used both by fresh acquisition and by a stale reclaimer's own final replacement write — could succeed inside that window and make a still-live replacement lock appear unlocked to a third caller, letting two holders run their callbacks concurrently. reclaimIfStale() holds and is blocked by the exact same reservation across its own claiming rename, for the identical reason: its rename likewise leaves the lock path briefly absent, and a concurrent tryCreate() succeeding inside that window (rather than deferring to whichever holder's content reclaimIfStale ultimately restores or replaces) would break exclusivity the same way. Both release()'s and reclaimIfStale()'s own claimed-content files use fixed, well-known paths once the shared reservation is held (never randomized), since the reservation itself already guarantees only one of the two is ever in flight for a given lock path at a time. If the process holding the reservation crashes before its own finally removes it, tryCreate() (and reclaimIfStale(), and release()) first check the marker's age against staleLockMs — the same abandoned-holder threshold governing the lock file itself. This reclaim is itself atomic, not a plain stat-then-unlink: the marker is claimed via its own atomic rename first, and only the *captured* file's own re-checked age (rename preserves mtime) decides whether to proceed, restoring it untouched if it turns out to be a fresh marker a different, legitimately live release()/reclaimIfStale() call created in the gap between the initial staleness check and this claim — a bare stat-then-unlink could otherwise strip that live call of its own protection mid-flight, the exact class of bug this whole mechanism exists to prevent. Once a claimed marker is confirmed genuinely stale, whichever fixed claim path holds orphaned content is restored back to the lock path via an exclusive-create write with the orphan's own original mtime reapplied afterward — never a plain renameSync, which POSIX silently allows to overwrite an existing destination file rather than fail (a concurrent, legitimate tryCreate() that already created a fresh lock at the lock path during this exact reclaim window, kept as narrow as an ordinary single ownership check since tryCreate() also recognizes the marker's own temporary '.reclaim' claim as blocking, must never be clobbered by the orphan), and reapplying the orphan's original mtime (rather than the fresh one an ordinary write would stamp) keeps its staleness signal intact so it re-enters the normal held/stale lifecycle immediately rather than needing a full extra staleLockMs wait to age out a second time — before the stale marker itself is dropped; without any of this, an abandoned reservation would otherwise block every future tryCreate() forever

occurredAt is validated identically for leap-second acceptance (23:59:60, in any offset) across control-plane.controlled-merge's own request validation, control-plane.evidence-store's schema validator, and control-plane.lifecycle-state-machine's own transition validation, so a leap-second timestamp accepted at entry can never fail deep in the pipeline after an irreversible merge or evidence write; 'in any offset' is checked by converting the local hour/minute to its UTC equivalent using the timestamp's own offset before comparing against 23:59, not by requiring the literal local digits to read 23:59, since a nonzero-offset leap second (for example '1990-12-31T15:59:60-08:00', the same instant as '...T23:59:60Z') need not
examples: a MERGE_READY task whose merge-readiness evaluate() reports ready=true, whose pull request is still open and unmerged at the approved revision on both the initial and immediate pre-merge checks, and whose merge provider confirms merged=true transitions MERGE_READY -> MERGED -> DONE, with one ipt.merge-evidence record naming the merge commit SHA
a MERGE_READY task whose merge-readiness evaluate() reports ready=false is rejected as NOT_MERGE_READY without ever calling the merge provider, and the task remains MERGE_READY
a MERGE_READY task whose pull request's head changes between the merge-readiness evaluation and the immediate pre-merge recheck is rejected as HEAD_CHANGED without calling the merge provider

a MERGE_READY task whose pull request is discovered already merged=true at the MERGE_READY-approved revision (a previous call's merge provider call succeeded but this controller crashed before recording evidence), with a base matching the configured integration target, is finalized directly from that confirmed result — no merge-readiness evaluation and no second mergePullRequest call occur

a MERGE_READY task with no MERGE_READY lifecycle-history event to search by at all, or whose merged candidate's base does not match the configured integration target, is not trusted via the shortcut; evaluate() is called normally and safely reports PULL_REQUEST_NOT_FOUND/NOT_MERGE_READY instead

a MERGE_READY task's confirmed merge is still discovered by the already-merged shortcut even after an unrelated push moved the branch's live head past the approved revision before evidence was recorded — the search key is the MERGE_READY-approved revision, not that new live head
a MERGED task (evidence and the MERGED transition already persisted, but lock release/DONE was interrupted) resumes purely from its persisted evidence with zero pull-request provider calls
a DONE task returns its persisted evidence unchanged on every subsequent call, with zero branch, provider, lock, or state-store writes
a merge provider call that fails outright (network error, non-2xx response) leaves the task MERGE_READY with no evidence recorded, safely retryable
an assignment lock already released by an earlier, successful completion attempt does not cause a later idempotent DONE-path call to fail
an assignment lock reassigned to a different actor's legitimate assignment between a fresh MERGE_READY attempt's entry and its completion step is left untouched: release() is never invoked for it

a MERGED task resumed after its original assignment was recovered as abandoned and reassigned to a different, legitimate actor releases nothing for that new actor: the identity read back from the original attempt's own persisted evidence never matches the now-active, differently-owned lock
a second merge() call for the same task while the first is still in its critical section is rejected as STATE_CONFLICT by the task lock rather than interleaving with the first

a merge() call whose readiness/provider calls run long enough to exceed the nominal stale-lock threshold is not reclaimed by a concurrent caller, because the held lock's heartbeat keeps refreshing its timestamp
a DONE task's merge() call completes without ever acquiring the task lock, even while a concurrent caller is actively holding it for a different, still-in-progress attempt on the same task

a pull request retargeted from the configured integrationTarget to a different base between merge-readiness evaluation and the pre-merge recheck is rejected as HEAD_CHANGED before the merge provider is called

a branch whose most-recently-created pull request (in any state) is an unrelated stray PR against a different base does not confuse the pre-merge recheck, since it fetches the readiness-selected PR by exact number rather than repeating the most-recent-by-head lookup

a crash between evidenceStore.record() succeeding and the MERGED lifecycle-state save persisting is resumed by reusing that exact already-recorded evidence rather than appending a second record for the same confirmed merge

a crash after mergePullRequest confirms the merge but before evidence is recorded is resumed correctly even when a stray, more-recently-created, unrelated PR now exists for the same branch, because crash recovery scans every candidate rather than only the most recent one

a more-recently-created merged pull request against an unrelated base, sitting ahead of the genuine integration-target merge for the same revision in the candidate list, does not shadow that genuine merge, since the base check is part of the selection predicate itself rather than a filter applied only after the first head-matching candidate is chosen

a genuinely merged pull request beyond the first 100 historical pull requests for a long-lived, reused branch is still discovered by crash recovery, since findPullRequestsByHead follows pagination rather than stopping at the first page

a later, unrelated evidence write to the same merge-evidence lineage (superseding the original as far as getCurrent() reports) does not change what a MERGED or DONE task's resume/idempotent-read resolves to, since resolution is pinned to the exact sequence the lifecycle-history event itself names

a lifecycle-history evidenceRef that is syntactically well-formed but names another task's merge-evidence lineage, or a record recorded against a different revision than the event itself claims, is rejected as EVIDENCE_REJECTED rather than trusted and cast
an evidence-store filesystem failure immediately after a confirmed merge is surfaced as a recoverable EVIDENCE_REJECTED, not a raw uncaught exception, leaving the confirmed merge safely resumable

an assignment lock whose lockId happens to be reused by a later, differently-owned assignment is not released by a call that only captured the original owner/run/branch, since release requires the full identity to match

an I/O failure reading the concrete assignment-lock store's own state during completion is surfaced as a recoverable LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED, not a raw uncaught exception, leaving the already-persisted MERGED state resumable

an I/O failure reading the concrete assignment-lock store's own state at merge entry (for a fresh MERGE_READY attempt) is likewise surfaced as a recoverable LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED before any branch, evidence, or provider work begins, leaving the task MERGE_READY and safely retryable
a raw throw from the concrete lock store's own release() call (as opposed to a well-formed rejection result) is surfaced as a recoverable LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED rather than propagating uncaught
a heartbeat-refreshed lock is never observably absent from its lock path while its holder is still active, so an ordinary concurrent acquire() for the same task can never succeed mid-heartbeat

a holder whose lock has been lost to a concurrent reclaim aborts at the assertHeld fencing check immediately before the merge provider call, before ever invoking mergePullRequest a second time for the same task

a holder that still holds the lock through the merge provider call but loses it in the narrow gap between finalize()'s evidence write and the MERGE_READY -> MERGED save aborts at that specific checkpoint, leaving the newly recorded evidence orphaned but the lifecycle state still MERGE_READY and safely retryable — never advancing to MERGED without the lock actually held at that exact write

finalize()'s reuse path for a task whose original assignment was recovered and reassigned before this retry ran releases nothing for the replacement actor, because the identity used for release() comes from the reused record's own assignmentLockAtMerge, not this retry's fresh live snapshot of a lock it does not actually own

a readiness-selected pull request that is closed (not merged) by the time of the immediate pre-merge recheck is rejected locally as HEAD_CHANGED, never passed to the merge provider only to be rejected there

a lock record whose identity still matches this call's captured identity, but whose status already reads RELEASED from an interrupted prior release call, is passed to release() again rather than skipped — completing the interrupted audit/archive steps (or, if the underlying failure persists, surfacing a fresh LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED) instead of abandoning that record forever
edgeCases: an unregistered taskId is rejected as TASK_NOT_FOUND
a non-schema-valid taskId, or an empty/untrimmed actorId, runId, or occurredAt, is rejected as INVALID_REQUEST before any dependency is touched
a task in any lifecycle state other than MERGE_READY, MERGED, or DONE (for example IN_DEVELOPMENT or QA_REVIEW) is rejected as TASK_STATE_NOT_MERGEABLE
a Git branch mismatch reported by the branch adapter is normalized to BRANCH_REJECTED rather than propagating a raw BranchLifecycleError
a merge-readiness evaluate() call that itself throws is normalized to MERGE_PROVIDER_FAILED
a merge-readiness result whose own resolved revision differs from the revision this controller already resolved is rejected as HEAD_CHANGED before ready is inspected
a confirmed already-merged pull request whose head SHA does not match the approved revision is rejected as HEAD_CHANGED rather than finalized against an unapproved commit
a confirmed already-merged pull request reporting merged=true with a null or empty-string merge commit SHA is rejected as MERGE_NOT_CONFIRMED

a MERGED or DONE task whose lifecycle history has no MERGED/DONE-toState event at all, or whose event's evidenceRef is malformed, or whose exact named sequence no longer exists in the evidence history (a state this module's own writes never produce, since evidence and its history event are always written before the corresponding lifecycle transition persists) is rejected as EVIDENCE_REJECTED rather than silently completing without a verifiable audit trail
rejected merge evidence (a schema-validation failure) is surfaced as EVIDENCE_REJECTED and blocks the lifecycle transition entirely
a lock-release rejection other than LOCK_NOT_FOUND/LOCK_ID_MISMATCH is surfaced as LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED, which still leaves the already-persisted MERGED state and evidence resumable

a MERGED task's evidence record whose assignmentLockAtMerge field is absent (older data), null, or malformed in any way resolves to 'nothing to release' rather than throwing or guessing at an identity to release

an attempt to record ipt.merge-evidence whose assignmentLockAtMerge is a bare string, number, boolean, or array — neither the declared object shape nor null — is rejected as SCHEMA_VALIDATION_FAILED by the evidence store's own type-array-aware validator, rather than silently accepted and later misread as 'no lock was active'

a non-strictly-RFC-3339 occurredAt — including a syntactically-shaped but calendar-invalid one such as February 29 on a non-leap year, day 31 of a 30-day month, hour 24, or a timezone offset of +24:00/+01:60, all of which Date.parse() silently rolls forward rather than rejecting — is rejected as INVALID_REQUEST before any branch, readiness, or provider call, using the same component-range (including offset-range) validation control-plane.evidence-store's own record()-time check uses, never discovered only later when that stricter check rejects it after an irreversible merge already happened

GitHub's list-pull-requests response (used by findPullRequestsByHead) exposes merged_at, not the merged boolean the single-pull-request endpoint returns; merged is derived as merged_at !== null so a real list-endpoint result is never rejected as malformed

a stale controlled-merge task-lock file (its filesystem mtime older than the same 5-minute threshold BOOT-018's/BOOT-019's/BOOT-020's/BOOT-021's own task locks use) is reclaimed by the next caller rather than wedging the task indefinitely if a prior holder crashed mid-merge; a live holder's periodic heartbeat keeps that same mtime fresh via a metadata-only touch, never a content rewrite

a GitHub merge response reporting merged=true with an empty-string sha (rather than a missing one) is rejected as PROVIDER_ERROR at the GitHub adapter boundary, before the controller ever treats it as confirmed

expectations: BOOT-026+ can drive a MERGE_READY task to DONE by calling merge() once per attempt, trusting NOT_MERGE_READY/HEAD_CHANGED/MERGE_PROVIDER_FAILED/MERGE_NOT_CONFIRMED as exact, safely-retryable reasons a call did not reach DONE, without the orchestrator itself needing to re-derive merge readiness, re-check the pull request head, or track whether a prior attempt already merged
acceptedRanges: a ControlledMergeResult with lifecycleState 'DONE' for a task that was MERGE_READY, MERGED, or DONE on entry
a thrown ControlledMergeError whose code and recoverable flag say whether retrying merge() unchanged can succeed
requiredReachableRanges: DONE is reachable for a task whose merge-readiness genuinely holds and whose pull request genuinely merges

every non-DONE outcome leaves the task's persisted lifecycle state unchanged from what merge() observed on entry, except a failure occurring after the MERGE_READY -> MERGED transition itself has already persisted — a lock-release failure (LOCK_RELEASE_FAILED), a lock lost to a concurrent reclaim at one of completeFromMerged()'s own fencing checks (STATE_CONFLICT), a rejected MERGED -> DONE transition (LIFECYCLE_REJECTED), or a failure persisting that transition (STATE_IO_FAILED) — any of which leaves the task at MERGED with evidence already persisted and safely resumable, never at an earlier state and never with evidence lost
